title: Al-Fattah, the Opener
hookLine: the Opener, of doors and of hearts
tomorrow: Amira has a worry she hasn't told anyone. who already knows?

lines: THANKS SO MUCH FOR ASKING, BUT.
cards: The email starts with "Thanks so much for asking, but." The owner said no to the outside wall. Two lines down, almost as an afterthought, he offered the long wall inside the shop.
Is that a no? A group of believers once got a no that looked much worse. With the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, they had set out for Mecca dressed as pilgrims, to visit the Kaaba.
At a place called Hudaybiyyah, they were stopped. A treaty was written. They would have to turn around and go home.

teach.b: Some of the companions found the terms hard to swallow. Umar was upset, and asked how they could accept this. They shaved their heads, made their sacrifices where they stood, and started home without reaching the Kaaba.
And on the road back, a surah came down.

teach.h: A SIGNAL VICTORY, ON THE WAY HOME.
teach.b: It opens, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! We have given thee (O Muhammad) a signal victory." The Arabic word is fath, an opening.
Umar asked, in a report in Sahih Muslim: is it a victory? And the answer came: yes. That's today's name.
Al-Fattah, the Opener, of doors and of hearts. Tradition remembers that the peace made at Hudaybiyyah opened ways that fighting had kept shut: people could travel, talk and listen to each other.
The door they wanted was closed. A wider one had opened, and it took a while to see it. The Qur'an puts the power plainly: "That which Allah openeth unto mankind of mercy none can withhold it."
Pickthall, in another verse, renders the same name as Judge, the One who opens the truth between people.
Here's what to tell a friend tonight: the surah named victory came down on the way home from a trip that didn't get where it was going.

how: Muslims recite surah al-Fath, named for the opening at Hudaybiyyah, and some call on Allah as ya Fattah when asking for a way forward.

o: the One who wins battles for His followers
the One who opens doors, hearts and ways forward
the One who closes every door that's wrong for you

games.q: the treaty and the opening — tap the pairs.
p: the Opener, of doors and hearts

s: the surah of victory came after a great battle was won
it came on the way home from Hudaybiyyah, after a treaty that looked like a setback.
Umar asked whether the treaty was really a victory
is it a victory? and the answer came: yes.
Pickthall renders al-Fattah in one verse as Judge
the One who opens the truth between people: the All-knowing Judge.

games.q: you're with the pilgrims at Hudaybiyyah. the treaty says turn back without reaching the Kaaba. what does the story have them do?
o: accept it, make their sacrifices where they are, and head home.
refuse the terms and push through to the Kaaba anyway.
wait at Hudaybiyyah until the terms are rewritten.
games.why: they turn back, and on the way home the surah calls it a signal victory: an opening they couldn't see yet.

practice: Choose one door in your life that seems shut right now: a job, a friendship, a conversation. Say it out loud, softly, in a few words.
If you pray, you can follow it with ya Fattah, O Opener, the name itself; if not, just say what you hope might open, and leave a little silence after it for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Fattah: the Opener, of doors and of hearts. At Hudaybiyyah, the opening came in the shape of a no.

orig.note: Arabic: the Opener, who opens doors, hearts, and the truth between people.

carryVoice: Here's the line: he opens, sometimes by way of a door that closed first. Until tomorrow.
